newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: First man dies under Australian suicide law.
newsitem.headline: First man dies under Australian suicide law.

text.p: An elderly Australian man dying of prostate cancer has become the world's first person to take his own life under a controversial voluntary euthanasia law, the doctor who assisted in his suicide said on Thursday.
News of the death surprised and outraged civil and religious leaders and renewed debate over a "mercy killing" law that many Australians, including Prime Minister John Howard, want to see quashed.

Dr Philip Nitschke told Reuters his patient died on Sunday from a lethal injection in Darwin, the capital of the remote Northern Territory, which residents fear could become the world's "Death Capital".

Nitschke said his computerised euthanasia system -- which asks a series of questions before administering the lethal drugs -- had been used in the death. But he would not say whether he or his patient, a man in his mid-60s who did not want to be named, pressed the buttons to administer the drugs.

"We made use of the computer software and the questions were answered and the machine delivered the medication," he told Reuters from Darwin. "The patient was expressing a sense of gratitude. He was as happy as someone could be under the circumstances."
Nitschke has been dubbed "Australia's Doctor Death" after Jack Kevorkian, the American doctor who has attended 40 suicides in his campaign to legalise euthanasia.

Nitschke said he felt sad but relieved at helping the man die. "You couldn't not be affected by it," he said. "It's a very difficult business ... and it's not the sort of thing you would want to make a habit of -- it certainly took its toll.
"I came out with a sense that I had done something good. There was also a bit of a sense of history."
Sydney's Roman Catholic archbishop, Edward Clancy, said the death was "a shameful day for Australia".

"At least this deplorable act may serve to bring the stark reality of euthanasia fully home to the consciousness of all Australians and further instances of this ugly evil may yet be prevented," he said in a statement.

Nitschke's patient wrote a letter the day before he died pleading with Australia's national parliament not to overturn the territory law, beset by controversy and a series of challenges since it came into operation on July 1.

"The church and state should be kept separate," the man wrote. "What right has anyone because of their own religious faith, to which I don't subscribe, to demand that I behave according to their rules and endure unnecessary intractable pain until some doctor in his omniscience decides that I have had enough and that he increases the morphine until I die.
"If you disagree with voluntary euthanasia, then don't use it, but please don't deny the right to me to use it if I want to."

A member of Howard's conservative government has launched a private action in parliament, with Howard's backing, which would see the national parliament use its constitutional powers to quash the territory law.
The challenge is the latest in a series of legal and political challenges that had delayed use of the law because doctors were unsure of their legal position.
Challenges in the territory parliament and the territory's Supreme Court have failed.

The law faces a separate threat in Australia's highest court, the High Court, where an anti-euthanasia coalition of doctors, church and Aboriginal leaders is seeking to have it declared unconstitutional.
Nitschke said that the man's death would help future assisted suicides. "The next one will be easier, it always gets easier," he said.
